# Governance

This document describes how decisions are made in Pulsar, who makes them, and what
a contributor can rely on. It describes the process that is actually in force, not
an aspiration: every mechanism named here is enforced by a gate, a test, or a file
in this repository, and each is linked so you can check.

## Project status and stewardship

Pulsar is currently maintained by a single steward, [@LennyObez](https://github.com/LennyObez).
Saying so plainly matters more than a governance structure that describes a
committee which does not exist. A one-person project has a real failure mode —
the bus factor is one — and the mitigations below are written with that in mind
rather than around it.

What that means for you in practice:

- Decisions are made quickly, and you will usually get an answer from the person
  who wrote the code.
- Review capacity is finite. A large unsolicited pull request may wait.
- Nothing important lives only in one person's head. The reasoning behind every
  architectural decision is written down before the code lands — see below.

If the project gains regular contributors, this document changes to match, and
that change will itself be an ADR.

## Architectural decisions are written before they are built

The load-bearing mechanism in this project is [`docs/adr/`](../docs/adr/): a
numbered, append-only series of Architecture Decision Records. There are more than
sixty.

[ADR-0001](../docs/adr/0001-ci-gates-and-adr-discipline.md) makes this binding:
**a change to a core architecture path requires a new or updated ADR**, and the
`ADR Governance Check` job enforces it on every pull request. It is a required
status check on `main`, so it is not advisory.

An ADR states the context, the decision, and the consequences — including the
consequences the author would rather not have. Several ADRs in this repository
exist specifically to record that an earlier decision was wrong and what replaced
it. That is the intended use.

**If you are proposing an architectural change, open an issue using the
[architecture proposal template](ISSUE_TEMPLATE/architecture-proposal.yml) first.**
Discussion happens on the issue; the ADR is written when the shape is agreed. This
saves you writing code against a design that will not be accepted.

## What is stable, and what is not

The public API surface is marked in code, not in documentation that can drift:

- `#[Api]` marks the stable surface. Once 1.0.0 is tagged, it is bound by
  [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).
- `#[Internal]` marks private machinery. It may change in any release.
- `\Internal\` namespaces are module-private and must not be imported across
  module boundaries.

That surface is recorded in [`tools/api/public-api.snapshot.json`](../tools/api/public-api.snapshot.json),
regenerated by `composer api:snapshot`, and a boundary check refuses a pull request
that crosses a module boundary it should not. The snapshot is committed precisely
so that a change to the public surface is a visible line in a diff rather than a
silent side effect.

During the release-candidate phase, **additive changes are preferred** and a
breaking change to an `#[Api]` type requires an ADR that argues for it.

## How a change reaches `main`

Every change arrives through a pull request. `main` is protected by a ruleset that
requires:

- **Signed commits.** Unsigned commits are refused; there is no exception.
- **Linear history.** No merge commits; the branch is squash-merged.
- **Six passing status checks**: PHP Quality (code style, PHPStan at max level,
  Psalm at level 1, module boundaries), JS/TS, PHP Tests, PHP and JS dependency
  audits, and the ADR Governance Check.
- **A current branch.** It must contain the tip of `main` at merge time.
- **Code scanning clean** at every alert level, and a **90% coverage floor**.

No force-pushes, no branch deletion. The full local equivalent is `composer qa`,
and `composer qa:parity` asserts that every gate in it is actually executed by the
CI workflow — so the gate you run locally and the gate that blocks your merge
cannot drift apart.

## The rule behind the rules

One principle governs more of this codebase than any other, and it explains
decisions that would otherwise look severe:

> A check that has never been observed to fail is indistinguishable from no check.

This is [ADR-0060](../docs/adr/0060-a-check-never-observed-to-fail-is-indistinguishable-from-no-check.md).
It is why several gates carry a _negative_ test that plants a defect and watches
the gate refuse it, and why suppression baselines are ratcheted: their counts are
recorded in [`tools/php/analysis-baseline-ceiling.json`](../tools/php/analysis-baseline-ceiling.json)
and may only shrink. Raising a ceiling is permitted — but it must be a deliberate
line in a diff that says so, never a silent side effect of regenerating a baseline.

That sentence was aspirational until 2026-09-02: the ceiling could be raised with
nothing else in the diff, because the only comparison anything made was the measured
count against whatever the file said. It is now enforced. Each ceiling records what it
replaced and why, and the reason has to _contain_ the current figure — so a number
cannot move without its justification being rewritten in the same commit. See
[ADR-0077](../docs/adr/0077-a-ceiling-is-a-ratchet-only-while-its-reason-names-the-number.md).

The same principle applies to what the framework claims about itself. A compliance
control reports what a deployment was _observed_ doing, never what its
configuration asks for; where nothing was measured, the report says "claimed and
not observed" rather than showing a pass. An audit that removes a false green is a
successful audit, even though the number goes down.

Expect review comments to ask _"what would make this fail?"_ more often than
_"does this work?"_.

## Roadmap and priorities

Work is tracked in [GitHub Issues](https://github.com/LennyObez/pulsar-framework/issues),
grouped by milestone, and planned on the delivery project board. Direction and
sequencing are in [`ROADMAP.md`](../ROADMAP.md).

Priority is set by the steward. The ordering principle is that correctness
defects outrank features, and defects in security, cryptography, or the compliance
evidence path outrank everything — this framework is built for regulated systems,
and a wrong answer there is worse than a missing one.

## Security decisions

Vulnerability handling follows [`SECURITY.md`](SECURITY.md) and is the one area
where discussion happens privately first. Report through GitHub Private
Vulnerability Reporting or the address in that file; please do not open a public
issue for a vulnerability.

Reporters are credited in the advisory unless they ask otherwise.

## Changing this document

Governance changes are themselves architectural decisions: propose one by opening
an issue, and the change lands as an ADR alongside the edit to this file. That is
deliberate. A governance document a maintainer can quietly rewrite is not
governance.
